params.prompt: Rosa, a self-employed electrician, applies for a medical plan. Her completed application and first premium are the offer. The insurer accepts by issuing the policy as applied for. If the insurer issues it with changes, that is a counteroffer she accepts by paying or keeping it. Consideration flows both ways: Rosa gives premium and truthful statements; the insurer gives its promise to pay covered expenses. Both parties must be competent, meaning of legal age and sound mind, and the contract must have a legal purpose. A contract missing any element is not enforceable.

Rosa did not negotiate the wording. The insurer wrote the policy and she took it or left it. That makes it a contract of adhesion, and courts read genuine ambiguities against the drafter, the insurer. The contract is also aleatory: the values exchanged are unequal and depend on chance. Rosa might pay small premiums and collect a large hospital bill, or pay for years and collect nothing. Neither party is cheated by that imbalance, because both agreed to accept it. These two characteristics explain why insurance disputes are decided differently from disputes over an ordinary purchase.

The policy is personal. It covers Rosa, and she cannot hand it to a neighbor; the insurer agreed to insure her health, not anyone’s. It is unilateral. Only the insurer makes an enforceable promise. Rosa is not legally required to keep paying, but if she stops, the promise lapses. It is conditional. The insurer’s duty to pay depends on conditions being met, such as premiums paid and proof of loss submitted on time. When a question asks why an insured cannot be sued for nonpayment, the answer is that the contract is unilateral.

Because the insurer drafted the contract, ambiguous language is interpreted the way a reasonable insured would understand it. The reasonable expectations doctrine goes a step further in some courts: coverage the buyer reasonably expected may be honored even if fine print says otherwise. Two more principles shape health insurance. Indemnity means the policy restores a loss but should not create profit, which is why medical expense plans reimburse actual charges. Utmost good faith means both sides must deal honestly. Rosa relies on the insurer’s solvency and wording; the insurer relies on her answers.

Rosa’s application answers are representations: statements she believes true. A material misrepresentation, one that would have changed the underwriting decision, lets the insurer rescind within the contestable period. A warranty is a statement guaranteed to be true, and in health insurance statements are treated as representations, not warranties, unless the policy says otherwise. Concealment is deliberately withholding a material fact the insurer did not ask about but should have been told. Fraud is intentional deception to gain a benefit. The difference is intent and materiality, and the remedies grow more severe along that line.

Suppose Rosa pays her premium twelve days late and the insurer accepts it without comment, then does so again. By voluntarily giving up its right to insist on prompt payment, the insurer has waived that right for those payments. Estoppel is the consequence: having led Rosa to rely on its conduct, the insurer is stopped from later denying a claim because a payment was late. Waiver is the voluntary surrender of a known right; estoppel prevents a party from reversing course after another relied on it. Together they keep insurers from using technicalities after their own conduct excused them.

Marcus and Elena list what could go wrong financially. Marcus could be too hurt to work, which is a loss of income. Anyone could face hospital and physician bills, which is medical expense. The children need cleanings and fillings, which is dental expense. Elena’s mother may someday need help with daily living, which is long-term care expense. Glasses and prescriptions are smaller, predictable costs. Each need has a matching benefit. Health insurance is a family of products, not one product, and the exam expects you to name the right member of the family for each loss.

Vision benefits usually cover an exam and an allowance toward lenses or frames on a schedule. Prescription drug benefits may be built into a medical plan or sold separately, with copayments that differ by drug tier. Specified disease, or dread disease, policies pay only if a named illness such as cancer is diagnosed, often as a lump sum or scheduled amount regardless of other coverage. They are supplements, not substitutes for medical insurance. A producer who presents a cancer policy as full health coverage misleads the buyer and may violate Maryland’s advertising rules.

AD and D pays a principal sum if an accident causes death, usually within a stated period after the injury. It pays a capital sum, often half the principal sum, for loss of a limb or sight in one eye, and typically the full principal sum for two such losses. It pays nothing for death from sickness. AD and D is sold alone, as a rider, or as part of group plans and travel coverage. Because the benefit is a fixed amount rather than reimbursement of bills, it is a valued benefit, and the accident definition in Lesson one decides whether it responds.

Rosa buys her own medical plan. The insurer underwrites her, she owns the policy and she pays the whole premium. That is individual coverage. Marcus is covered at work. His employer holds the master policy, he receives a certificate of coverage, the group is underwritten as a whole and the employer often pays part of the premium. That is group coverage. Group plans spread risk across the whole workforce, cost less per person to administer and have special rules about eligibility, continuation and conversion that we will study later. Individual plans follow the person wherever she goes.

Rosa’s and Marcus’s plans are private: a company accepts premium and promises benefits under a contract. Dennis, who turns sixty-five next year, will join Medicare, a federal program funded by payroll taxes and premiums. Gloria, his mother, might someday qualify for Medicaid if her savings run out. Social Security disability and workers compensation are also government programs. Private coverage is voluntary and contractual; government coverage is created by statute and open to people who meet the statutory tests. Many families hold both, and later lessons explain which pays first.

A comprehensive medical plan covers a wide range of hospital, surgical, physician and preventive services, subject to deductibles and coinsurance. A limited policy covers only a narrow peril or pays a small fixed amount: accident-only, hospital indemnity, specified disease, dental-only or vision-only. Limited policies are legitimate supplements, but Maryland requires them to disclose their limited nature so no one mistakes a two hundred dollars a day hospital policy for health insurance. When you classify a policy, use all three axes: individual or group, private or government, limited or comprehensive.
